title: The self to be trained
hook: the self that commands evil, that blames itself, that is at peace (12:53; 75:2; 89:27)

segments.voice: Yesterday, gathered remembrance: circles of dhikr, some rising like surf, some in total silence. Your line: the heart says it.

It's eleven at night. One voice in you says: one more episode, one more slice, send the angry text, you deserve it. Ten minutes later, another: why did you do that? You always do that. And once in a while, on a good day, there's a third thing, not really a voice at all. A quiet. You did the right thing, or you didn't and you've made it right, and you're simply at rest. Everyone knows those three. The Qur'an names them, in three different surahs, and Sufis built a whole map of the inner life on them.
screen: `ONE MORE, YOU DESERVE IT.` → `WHY DID YOU DO THAT?` → `A QUIET.`

segments.voice: The Arabic word is nafs: soul, self, or ego, depending on the sentence. The first nafs is in the story of Yusuf. In Pickthall's translation: "the (human) soul enjoineth unto evil," except where God has mercy. Commentators differ on who says those words, Yusuf or the wife of the man who bought him, but all agree on what they describe: the self that pushes, that grabs, that wants now. An-nafs al-ammarah, the self that commands. The second is in a short Meccan surah, where God swears an oath by it: "Nay, I swear by the accusing soul." An-nafs al-lawwamah, the self that blames: the voice at eleven-ten. God swears by it. The conscience that stings is honored, not despised. The third comes near the end of surah 89, addressed with great tenderness: "But ah! thou soul at peace!" An-nafs al-mutma'innah, the self at rest, invited to return to its Lord, content. Sufi teachers read the three as stages. The self isn't evil, and it isn't thrown away. It's trained, the way you'd train a strong young horse: not broken, but taught. The work of the path is moving from commanding, through blaming, toward peace. A hadith in al-Bukhari fits: the strong one isn't the one who wins the wrestling match, but the one who controls himself when angry. Train the self.
screen: `NAFS — SOUL, SELF, EGO.` · `THE SELF THAT COMMANDS.` · `THE SELF THAT BLAMES.` · `THE SELF AT PEACE.` · then, large: `TRAIN THE SELF.`

segments.voice: Replay your day so far and name each self that spoke: the commanding one, pushing for more, faster, now; the blaming one, stinging, maybe too harshly; and any moment of quiet, even a few seconds. Name them without judging them, and thank the blaming self for caring. If you pray, you can ask God to bring your self to peace.
Nafs. The self, in three stages in the Qur'an: commanding, blaming, and at peace. Today's word.
Your line: train the self. Not broken, but taught, like a strong young horse. Day three hundred six.

howItsDone: Muslims speak of struggling with the nafs as a lifelong part of faith, and Sufi teachers guide students through its stages, commanding, blaming and at peace, with remembrance, self-examination and service.

fork.reveal: nay, I swear by the accusing soul (75:2). the conscience that stings is honored, a stage on the way to peace.

what it means: the self has stages, commanding, blaming, at peace, and the path trains it, not destroys it.
what a scholar hears: ammarah (12:53), lawwamah (75:2), mutma'innah (89:27), three Qur'anic descriptions that Sufis arranged as stages.
